abstract: |
 A focus on legislative work has limited contemporary understanding of congressional representation. In this paper, we advance and measure a concept of interbranch representation --- how members of Congress work directly with federal agencies on behalf of various constituencies. Interbranch representation includes casework (constituency service) on behalf of individuals, nonprofits, and businesses, as well as engaging with executive branch policymaking and implementation. To explain stark variation in interbranch representation, we develop a unified framework of Demand, Capacity, and Motivation, which integrates and extends theories rooted in varying levels of demand for interbranch representation, unequal legislator capacity to deliver service, and varying strategic motivations to invest time and resources in interbranch representation rather than other activities. A large share of variation is explained by capacity, particularly staff resources and experience in Congress. We find evidence of partisan strategic behavior but little evidence that reelection motivation drives interbranch work.

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Scholarship on how members of the U.S. Congress represent their constituents has focused on legislative activity, including bill sponsorship [@Schiller95; @RoccaGordon2010; @Lazarus2013; @Waggoner2019; @LauterbachHayesWellerBishin2026; @YoelLucasGrossmann2026], roll-call votes [@rohde1991pal; @poolerose1997; @AnsSnySte2001LSQ; @AnsolabehereJones2010; @Wallace2014; @Fowler2026], committee participation [@Hall1987; @Hall1996; @Gamble2007; @EllisWilson2013; @BanGrimmerKaslovskyWest2022], and floor speeches [@MaltzmanSigelman1996; @Hill02; @PearsonDancey2011a; @PearsonDancey2011b; @Kalaf2020]. Importantly, all of these activities are highly visible to scholars, journalists, and constituents. While research on these activities has made valuable contributions, we argue that a focus on legislative work has limited contemporary understanding of congressional representation. How government affects one's constituents is not fully determined by votes and the text of bills that become law. Federal agencies staffed by career civil servants and political appointees do a large share of policymaking as well as all policy implementation. When Congress makes new laws, it instructs agencies to make and implement new policies. Even federal laws that empower state governments are almost always shaped and overseen by federal agencies. Given the prominent role of federal agencies in modern governance, it makes sense that members of Congress frequently involve themselves in executive-branch policymaking and implementation to help their constituents, advocate for their districts, and advance their policy goals. However, the relative invisibility of this involvement has made it an under-studied part of representation. We have thus failed to assess our democracy on important grounds. 

In this paper, we advance, measure, and explain the concept of **interbranch representation** --- how Members of Congress work directly with federal agencies on behalf of various constituencies. Interbranch representation includes casework (constituency service) on behalf of individuals, nonprofits, and businesses as well as communicating with agencies about executive-branch policymaking and implementation. For example, prior work shows how legislators engage in interbranch representation to represent constituents' needs [@Fiorina1977; @Fenno1978; @MillsKalafHughes2015; @PowellJudgeLordGrimmer2023; @SnyderJudgeLordPowellGrimmer2025], constituents' policy preferences [@Ritchie2018; @Ritchie2023], shared identity groups <small>[@LowandeRitchieLauterbach2019], or corporate donors [@PowellJudgeLordGrimmer2023]. 

To study interbranch representation comprehensively, we leverage a new dataset that includes over half a million hand-coded requests sent from Members of Congress to federal agencies between 2007 and 2025. We obtained these data by filing 434 Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests for all incoming communication from members of Congress. These painstakingly collected new data allow us to systematically measure representation in a new way. <!--more about data here-->

<!--the paragraph below is what I think articulates the main story we are trying to tell-->

We show that interbranch representation is common but varies widely across members of Congress: some provide a great deal to their constituents, while others provide almost none. To explain why members of Congress engage in interbranch representation, we offer a unified framework that integrates and extends theories rooted in unequal **demand**, unequal legislator **capacity**, and varying **strategic motivations** to invest time and energy in interbranch representation as opposed to other activities like legislating, communications, or fundraising. Theoretically and empirically, the capacity of congressional offices is at the center of this framework. Unequal capacity consistently explains legislators’ interbranch work across a variety of domains. Constituent demand and legislator strategy play important roles in shaping which constituents are served, but have smaller effects on the amount of interbranch representation that a district receives. The strategic behavior we do see is associated with partisan/ideological and institutional context, not electoral incentives. 

These findings have implications for the study of representation in Congress, particularly how scholars conceive of the role of congressional staff and the extent to which representation is unconstrained by legislative agendas and party discipline. The role of congressional staff in interbranch work also speaks to how representation can be improved. More generally, because policy implementation is how the public interacts with government and experiences policy effects, the involvement of members of Congress at this stage of the process matters for representation. 

We begin by defining our concept of interbranch representation and reviewing existing research that has studied related concepts in @sec-concept. We then introduce a three-part framework of Demand, Capacity, and Strategy that unifies and extends this work [@sec-framework]. @sec-design presents our research design, measurement strategy, and statistical models. We then present results in @sec-results, showing that Demand, Capacity, and Strategy all play a role in explaining interbranch representation, with Capacity foremost among them. @sec-conclusion concludes with a discussion of our findings' implications for research on representation and congressional capacity. 

# What is Interbranch Representation? {#sec-concept}

Interbranch representation broadly involves officials of one branch representing their constituents in decision-making processes of another branch. This broad concept of interbranch representation includes oversight hearings and amicus briefs that legislators file in court as well as the focus of this paper: requests from congressional offices to federal agencies.

Scholars have studied parts of interbranch representation under labels including "congressional oversight," "constituency service" [@Fenno1978], "lettermarking" in the context of spending [@MillsKalafHughes2015], "lobbying," "backchannel representation," "backdoor lawmaking," or "policy representation" in the context of agency policymaking [@Ritchie2018; @Ritchie2023; @RitchieYou2019; @LauterbachRitchie2025], "legislator advocacy" in the context of both constituent and donor service [@PowellJudgeLordGrimmer2023], "interbranch representation" in the context of legislators advising agency working groups [@USDepartmentofJustice2016], and "interbranch representation of protected groups" in the context of descriptive representation in contacts to the bureaucracy [@LowandeRitchieLauterbach2019], or simply "representation" in the context of all types of requests to the bureaucracy [@JudgeLordPowellGrimmer2026]. We adopt "interbranch representation" as a general umbrella concept to describe all of these kinds of representational activities, not only working group participation or contacts on behalf of descriptive identities, but also work on behalf of any other constituency, donor, business, industry, or district opinion on policy issues with another branch of government. 

We conceptualize interbranch representation as varying along two dimensions: the constituency represented (e.g., individuals, businesses, nonprofits, or local governments) and the type of representational activity undertaken (e.g., constituency service or policy work). This yields five sub-types of interbranch representation: (1) constituency service work on behalf of individual constituents, (2) constituency service work on behalf of businesses, (3) constituency service work on behalf of local governments or nonprofits, (4) general policy work with federal agencies, and (5) policy work with federal agencies on behalf of specific industries.^[While it is possible to identify policy benefiting particular industries, we created a "general" category for all of the policy work because we found it impossible to distinguish policy work done on behalf of individuals, nonprofits, or local governments].

 <!--Rochelle 8/19: can also include some qualitative examples here if we think we have enough space?-->

To date, the activities that constitute these five sub-types of interbranch representation have been addressed by separate literatures. Constituency service has mostly been explored as reelection-oriented behavior [@CainFerejohnFiorina1987], and until recently [e.g. @Snyder2024; @Blackwood2026], scholars have not considered how it can function as part of representation. Scholarship on the interaction between Congress and the executive branch has revolved around the concepts of strategic delegation of policymaking authority and appropriation of funds on the front end [@Arnold1979; @EpsteinOHalloran1999; @KiewietMcCubbins1991] and oversight on the back end [@McCubbinsSchwartz1984]. <!--As a concept, delegation focuses attention on principal-agent dynamics. Oversight scholarship has also focused on principal-agent relationships, with some recent work on descriptive representation [@Minta2011].  While interbranch representation encompasses many forms of oversight, it is broader than activities traditionally considered oversight (e.g., hearings, investigations, sanctions). --> However, only a small share of congressional interactions with bureaucrats concern issues that rise to the level of hearings and investigations (the focus of most oversight scholarship). The vast majority are interventions in the agency's day-to-day operations [see, e.g., @Lowande2018APSR; @LowandePotter2021]. Agencies are constantly engaged in maintaining their political coalitions and reputations [@Carpenter2001; @Carpenter2014], tagging all incoming requests from members of Congress as "VIP" and implementing protocols for rapid responses. An interbranch representation perspective broadens the concept of oversight to encompass not only occasional hearings and oversight reports prompted by crises and scandals but also daily requests for information and comments on implementation. Overall, the concept of interbranch representation that we advance in this paper unifies constituency service, oversight, and other behaviors within a broader conceptual and empirical framework. 

Unlike other, more visible forms of congressional representation that have been the subject of substantial scholarly inquiry (roll-call votes, legislative speech, and bill sponsorship), interbranch representation is largely invisible and more difficult to study. Congress has refused to disclose data on this aspect of its work. In recent years, however, scholars have begun to obtain snapshots of this work from federal agencies that are (unlike Congress) subject to the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) disclosure requirements. Acquiring these data is difficult, but doing so has yielded important findings on distributive politics [@MillsKalafHughes2015], descriptive representation [@LowandeRitchieLauterbach2019], agency policymaking [@Ritchie2018, and @Ritchie2023], legislative effectiveness [@KalafHughes2023], and money in politics [@PowellJudgeLordGrimmer2023]. <!--However, the lack of systematic data across all policy areas and agencies has necessarily limited the range of questions that could be explored with these data.--> <!--Rochelle 8/19: this last sentence doesn't really fit well with this paragraph anymore; alternatively, we could move this whole paragraph to the intro somewhere?-->

The particular instance of contact between congressional offices and federal agencies is just one stage in the process by which interbranch representation occurs. To further illuminate the theory that we discuss below, it is necessary to describe the processes that produce interbranch representation. Because it involves both constituency service and policy work, much of interbranch representation may begin with a constituent becoming aware of some deficiency in the world and understanding it as a problem---particularly, a problem in which the federal government has a hand in either solving or creating. Second, the individual recognizes that congressional offices can help with this problem. Third, they contact a congressional office, which constitutes the *demand* part of our theory explaining interbranch representation. Fourth, the congressional office processes the request (per their *capacity*) and decides how to handle the request (in accordance with any *strategy* that they may wish to exercise). Finally, for the subset of cases for which such an action is appropriate and desired by the congressional office, the office will contact a federal agency. Our data capture these instances of contact. 

Two other key features of interbranch representation are important to discuss further. First, as established above, legislators have a significant amount of discretion and autonomy in their decisions about engaging in interbranch representation, including where and how to direct these efforts. Party leaders constrain most other activities that legislators undertake, and even other activities where this constraint matters less, like position-taking, are highly public [e.g. @HightonRocca2005]. Explaining why legislators engage in interbranch representation can therefore provide rich insight into congressional behavior that, given the importance of party and party leadership, previous work has largely been unable to reveal. Second, congressional staff are as important as legislators themselves for the activities that constitute interbranch representation. Staff are crucial for a number of functions in Congress [e.g. @HertelFernandez2019; @MontgomeryNyhan2017; @CrossonEtAl2020], particularly constituent-facing functions like constituency service [@GroseMangumMartin2007; @LandgraveWeller2020]. Similarly, legislators themselves do not personally undertake all of the interbranch representation activities that they perform. Thus, our theory focuses as much on the capacity and other characteristics of the congressional *office* as it does on the decisions and characteristics of legislators. In the following section, we explain our unified framework of Demand, Capacity, and Strategy in greater depth. 

# A Unified Framework: Demand, Capacity, and Strategy {#sec-framework}

We introduce a framework of Demand, Capacity, and Strategic Motivations to extend and unify theoretical ideas from disparate strands of scholarship on Congress and the bureaucracy. Demand- and capacity-related explanations focus on congressional offices as bureaucracies, with routines for processing inputs and outputs determined by the allocation of limited capacity, such as staffing levels and expertise. Strategic explanations focus on legislators as politicians. @fig-causal shows how demand, capacity, and strategy shape the work that congressional offices produce.^[@fig-causal shows these relationships at the highest level of abstraction. @fig-causal2 provides additional detail.] 

```{r}

#| fig-cap: "How constituent demand, capacity, and strategy shape interbranch representation activities"
#| out-width: "80%"
#| 
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "mermaid-figure-1.png"))
```

In the following sections, we elaborate on each of these components of our framework. 

## Demand

We define *Demand* as the constituent-driven influences on a congressional office. In any democratic system, the needs and preferences of a legislator's constituents are at least supposed to play a role in the work done by a legislator's office. While a large literature exists examining whether and how constituents' policy preferences impact legislators' voting behavior [@MillerStokes1963; @AchenBartels2016], less is known about how constituent demand relates to the provision of interbranch representation. <!--Of all work done by congressional offices, one might imagine that interbranch representation, in which a large portion of the work is helping individual constituents navigate specific problems they have encountered with some branch of the federal bureaucracy, might be most closely tied to constituent demand. One of the central elements of interbranch representation---constituency service---is often assumed to be a core institutional function of congressional offices, as evidenced by the fact that district office staff continue to provide constituency service even when the congressional office is vacant due to the death or resignation of the legislator. This dynamic suggests that constituency service is an activity aptly described by the "logic of appropriateness" that characterizes bureaucracies [@MarchOlsen1989]. Extending this idea to the realm of interbranch representation, legislators and their staff provide service to constituents simply because it is understood to be a key part of their representational responsibilities. Staff in particular understand their job to be responding to all constituent requests. --> 


::: {#thm-hyp:demand}
## Demand
Legislators with more constituent demand will do more interbranch representation. 
:::

## Capacity 

We turn next to the capacity component of our theory. We define *Capacity* as the ability of a legislator's office to produce work. We argue that the amount of interbranch representation that legislators engage in is likely to be positively associated with the capacity of the legislator's office. Congressional offices with greater capacity have the potential to provide more interbranch representation, while the inverse is true for offices with less capacity. We are building on four branches of capacity literature: (1) formal theory voter screening models that predict that as a legislator's capacity increases, they will increase their level of constituency service [@AshworthBuenodeMesquita2006], (2) empirical research that suggests low congressional capacity serves as a major constraint on Congress's work [@LaPiraDrutmanKosar2020; @Reynolds2020; @BoltonThrower2016; @BoltonThrower2022], (3) empirical research that shows legislator capacity impacts backchannel (backdoor) policymaking  ---  when legislators contact executive agencies attempting to influence policy [@Ritchie2018; @Ritchie2023], and (4) our prior research that shows that increases in congressional capacity can offset shifts in legislator priorities between policymaking and constituency service [@JudgeLordPowellGrimmer2026].

::: {#thm-capacityunequal}
## Capacity
Congressional offices with more capacity will do more interbranch representation. 
:::



## Strategy

We define *Strategy* as decisions legislators make about what to prioritize and how to allocate their time and resources in response to the political environment (partisan, electoral, and institutional incentives a member faces in a given year). How much energy and staff time do legislators want to devote to interbranch representational activities as opposed to other tasks like legislating, communicating, and fundraising? Similarly, how much time and energy do they want to devote to different types of interbranch representational activities? We argue that the answer depends on the strategic choices legislators make in response to their political environment. 

Beginning with @Fenno1973 and @Mayhew1974, a substantial body of literature on the U.S. Congress has explored the strategic choices. We build on existing literatures to hypothesize how legislators will strategically respond to variation in the partisan/ideological [@BerryBurdenHowell2010], electoral [@Fenno1973; @Mayhew1974; @Fiorina1977; @CainFerejohnFiorina1987; @SerraCover1992; @SerraMoon1994; @DroppPeskowitz2012], and institutional environment [@Lowande2019; @LowandePotter2021; @Ritchie2023].  

### Electoral Incentives

While it is difficult to measure a legislator's motivation directly, we can identify situations in which legislators are likely to prioritize certain goals or motivations. Perhaps the most widely recognized strategic motivation of legislators is reelection [e.g., @Mayhew1974; @CainFerejohnFiorina1987; @Fiorina1977; @Fenno1973]. As David Mayhew famously wrote in *Congress: The Electoral Connection*, "[Reelection] has to be the *proximate* goal of everyone, the goal that must be achieved over and over if other ends are to be entertained" [@Mayhew1974]. Legislators motivated by electoral concerns might devote additional attention and resources to helping their constituents, so that those constituents will vote to reelect the legislator [@SerraCover1992; @SerraMoon1994; @DroppPeskowitz2012 ]. Yet, in the modern Congress, very few members of Congress are electorally vulnerable in either general or primary elections. Legislators who do find themselves in an electorally vulnerable political environment are likely to prioritize reelection. Legislators motivated by electoral concerns might devote additional attention and resources to helping their constituents, so that those constituents will vote to reelect the legislator [@Dodd1977; @Fiorina1977; @CainFerejohnFiorina1987; @SerraCover1992; @SerraMoon1994; @DroppPeskowitz2012]. 

Members of Congress purport to believe that constituency service work will help their reelection efforts, with 44% of members saying they believed reelection was the primary reason most members perform constituency service [@Johannes1984, pg. 13]. This intuition has some empirical grounding. In their exploration of why Americans like their individual member of Congress more than Congress the institution (what has become known as Fenno's paradox), @ParkerDavidson1979 found that Americans evaluate the institution of Congress based on its legislative performance, the style and pace of the legislative process, and legislative-executive relations. At the same time, they judge individual members of Congress on the basis of two factors: constituency service and the legislator's personal characteristics. 

This expectation that electorally vulnerable legislators will do more constituency service, however, is contrary to Ritchie's findings in *Backdoor Lawmaking* about a different form of interbranch representation---policy work with federal agencies---which showed no consistent relationship between electoral vulnerability and policy work with federal agencies [@Ritchie2023]. 

Another potential reason for caution regarding the relationship between electoral vulnerability and interbranch representation is the invisibility of interbranch representation. Although reelection motives have long been posited as a motivation to engage in constituency service, a skeptic might question whether allocating time and resources to a largely invisible activity rather than something more visible like communications or legislation is the best strategy. While acts of constituency service might be visible to an individual who has been helped, as well as their friends and family, one would have to assume fairly large social network amplification effects for it to reach enough voters to make an electoral difference at a time when the size of the average House district is over 760,000 people [@CRSCensus2026].

### Partisanship and Ideology 

If interbranch work focuses on procuring benefits for constituents, we should see more work among partisan and ideological allies. 
For example, members of the President's party receive more federal spending in their districts [@BerryBurdenHowell2010]. Expecting relatively greater success, members of the President's party may thus engage in higher levels of interbranch representation. Interbranch representation is at the nexus of the Congress and the executive branch. The behavior we are documenting in this book is the congressional portion of that relationship; it is legislators reaching out to executive branch agencies. To actually deliver results to their constituents, the agencies need to cooperate. If legislators of the President's party think they are more likely to receive higher levels of cooperation from executive branch agencies, they may be motivated to attempt interbranch representation at higher rates. 

A similar logic of working with friends and receiving a warmer reception applies for agencies that are ideologically closer to the legislators. This may be in part because of the way that party coalitions represent interests. For example, the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) may be perceived as conservative in part because it represents Republican-dominated rural states, and the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) may be perceived as liberal because it represents more urbanized states dominated by Democrats. If interbranch work is about procuring benefits, we would expect rural representatives to work more with USDA and urban representatives to work more with HUD, thus producing a pattern of interbranch work favoring allies in one's policymaking and implementing coalition. 

Alternatively, if interbranch work focuses more on oversight than procuring benefits for constituents, we might see the opposite. While members of the president's party might anticipate a friendlier reception from executive branch agencies controlled by a same-party president, members of the opposition party might have greater incentives to engage in oversight of an executive branch controlled by an opposing party's president [but see @Lowande2018APSR]. Similarly, we might anticipate constituents of opposition party legislators having more concerns or problems with agencies more associated with a president of a different party, who might prioritize different types of constituents or policies less hospitable to opposition party constituents. Lastly, Ritchie's argument that legislators turn to backdoor policymaking when they confront obstacles in the legislative process applies here, too. Faced with a president unlikely to support the legislative proposals of opposition legislators, Ritchie found that legislators were more likely to turn to backchannel policymaking [@Ritchie2023].

Party coalitions suggest some divergence with respect to which constituencies legislators represent, with Republicans typically perceived as being friendlier to business interests [@GimpelLeeParrott2014]. Ideology may also matter for legislators' interbranch representation, as more bipartisan (and therefore more ideologically moderate, per DW-NOMINATE scores) legislators are more effective at pursuing their policymaking goals through lawmaking [@HarbridgeVoldenWiseman2023]. <!--The same logic could apply to interbranch representation, with more ideologically extreme legislators doing less of this work. Given the Republican Party's orientation toward smaller government, which has been particularly pronounced in its more extreme Tea Party and Freedom Caucus wings in recent years, ideologically extreme Republicans may be uniquely predisposed to avoid working with federal agencies, including through interbranch representation. Because ideologically extreme Democrats generally favor *more* government action and involvement, we would not expect to see such an effect for all ideologically extreme legislators.

### Institutional Incentive Structures

Layered on top of ideological/partisan coalitions are chamber rules and the institutional structure of Congress that empowers certain legislators based on their committee assignments and party caucus. 
If legislators anticipate that agencies under the jurisdiction of their committee would be more responsive to their requests^[It is beyond the scope of this paper to ascertain the validity of this assumption---whether the agencies are actually more responsive to committee members---and at least one study [@MillsKalafHughes2015] found no support for this intuition.], then we might expect these legislators to make more requests of these agencies.

**Strategy**
The political environment (partisan, electoral, institutional, and ideological context) shapes the strategic choices legislators make about how much and what forms of interbranch representation to invest in.  

**Hypothesis 3a (Partisan/Ideological):**  The partisan/ideological environment shapes the strategic choices legislators make about how much and what forms of interbranch representation to invest in. However, as discussed above, partisan/ideological incentives could have opposing effects depending on whether interbranch work is mostly collaborative policymaking and implementation or antagonistic oversight.

- **Hypothesis 3a(+): Partisan/Ideological Alignment**: Legislators from the President's party will do more interbranch work overall, and those who are ideologically aligned with an agency will engage in higher amounts of interbranch representation with that agency.
- **Hypothesis 3a(-): Partisan/Ideological Antagonism**: Legislators opposing party of the President will do more interbranch work overall, and those who are ideologically *distant* from an agency will engage in higher amounts of interbranch representation with that agency.
- **Hypothesis 3a(business): Partisan Coalition**: Republicans will do more interbranch representation of businesses interests.

**Hypothesis 3b (Electoral):** Legislators worried about reelection (from more electorally vulnerable districts) will do more interbranch representation

**Hypothesis 3c (Institutional):** Legislators will invest more in activities where their institutional positions give them leverage; conversely, they will invest less in activities where their institutional position puts them at a disadvantage.

# Data and Research Design {#sec-design}

To understand highly unequal levels of interbranch representation, we rely on a nearly decade-long data collection effort to look both descriptively at cross-sectional differences across legislators and more rigorously at within-legislator and within-district differences-in-differences specifications for causal leverage. While in an ideal world we would be able to look at our more rigorous specifications in all circumstances, some of our hypotheses can only be examined descriptively. 



## Measuring Interbranch Representation

Since 2017, we have been filing FOIA requests with all federal agencies and sub-agencies for all records of their correspondence with members. This effort to collect a near census of legislator-agency interactions has yielded by far the largest and most comprehensive dataset of its kind. We requested records from 295 federal agencies and received records from	179. Thousands of pages of agency logs yielded 962,720 instances of what agencies tagged as congressional correspondence, 837,223 of which we link to a legislator in office at the time.^[The remainder are committee staff, state legislators, judges, agency officials, lobbyists, White House officials, former members of Congress, or future members of Congress and others who were, for various reasons, swept into an agency's tracking systems or search for records. In some cases, agencies appeared to use their congressional correspondence tracking system as a general for VIPs. The Department of Education included Politico correspondent Jennifer Haberkorn and Kenneth P Vogel from the New York Times. The Federal Highway Administration tagged 27 letters from a particularly well-connected consultant. A smaller number are members of Congress whose names were ambiguous, illegible, or inappropriately redacted. ] 

We spent an even greater effort on hand-coding nearly all of these records—over half a million legislator requests to federal agencies—to capture whom the legislator was advocating on behalf of in each instance. This effort gives us high confidence in the quality of the data we use to make inferences. From these new data emerged a new picture of what legislator offices do and how they interact with the executive branch that demanded rethinking our understanding of representation and the institutions of American democracy. For more on our data collection and coding process, see @sec-appendix-methods. For summary statistics, see @sec-appendix-data.

Obtaining records of legislators’ communications with federal agencies through FOIA requests is laborious, painstaking, and time-consuming, with agencies often taking years to respond to a single request.  We have spent hundreds of hours negotiating with FOIA officers, filing appeals, and convincing judges to order agencies to provide these documents. The raw data we received (often scanned PDFs full of redactions, handwritten call logs, or screenshots of database entries) has taken years to clean and process. Understandably, therefore, recent studies have focused on records from a limited number of agencies. Those studies have yielded important findings regarding distributive politics [@MillsKalafHughes2015], the policy strategies of cross-pressured legislators [@Ritchie2018; @Ritchie2023], the role of ideology in congressional oversight [@Lowande2019], descriptive representation [@LowandeRitchieLauterbach2019], and money in politics [@PowellJudgeLordGrimmer2023]. With a near census of agencies, we are able to study patterns across all members and policy areas. This allows us to ask more general questions, test existing explanations out of sample, and compare the magnitude of effects documented in previous studies.

These data (an order of magnitude greater than those in all prior studies combined) enable us to address a range of new questions about representation that previous studies, which focused on a small number of agencies, could not. <!--Our data allows us to quantify the nature of the contact, but also includes rich data on the content of those contacts. -->

## Measuring Demand

Predicting and measuring demand for interbranch representation, particularly for constituency service, is difficult given the variety of activities and types of service that it encompasses. In the simplest and most general sense, we can think of demand for interbranch representation as depending on the number of constituents in a legislator's district or state. Beyond population, however, demand for individual constituency service can be thought of as arising from the confluence of several different factors: the amount of interaction that a legislator's constituents have with the federal government; the problems that arise from these interactions with government; constituents' knowledge of legislators' ability to help them navigate these problems; and the ability of constituents to advocate for their interests. Even when accounting for the number of constituents who use federal programs, it is nearly impossible to accurately predict the problems that constituents might encounter through their use of these programs. Further complicating this picture is that legislators appear to use capacity to generate demand through advertising and informing their constituents about ways they can help---either for strategic reasons or just because they believe normatively it is the right thing for them to do.

While we are not able to precisely measure demand in the form of actual problems that constituents experience with federal agencies or the number of constituent requests that legislators' offices receive, we are able to measure demand in three broader ways: **the number**, **neediness**, and **political savvy** of constituents. We use demographic estimates from U.S. Census Bureau data [@tidycensus] to calculate our three types of demand measures. 

To measure the **number** of constituents, we use the estimated population of states and congressional districts. The first and most straightforward component of constituent demand is the number of constituents. We view this as a mechanical relationship. If X proportion of constituents encounter problems with the federal government, the more constituents one represents, the more constituents one will represent encountering problems with the federal government. While the number of constituents represented by United States Representatives is roughly equivalent, U.S. Senators represent states with a wide range of state populations. The more people a legislator represents, the more problems they are likely to encounter with the federal government, and thus the greater demand for interbranch representation. While an intuitive argument, little empirical evidence exists to support it. @Johannes1984 found a weak positive relationship between state population and senators' constituency service caseloads in the late 1970s.  

While not explicitly focused on the issue of constituency demand, there is a body of research examining the impact of state population (constituency size) on Senate representation, demonstrating the opposite relationship between population and representation [@Oppenheimer1996; @Lee1998; @LeeOppenheimer1999]. Perhaps of greatest relevance, @Oppenheimer1996 found that constituents from more populous states have less contact with their legislators across a variety of survey measures (meeting the incumbent personally, attending a meeting where the incumbent spoke, speaking with a staff member, receiving mail from the incumbent, and contacting the incumbent). Of particular interest for our purposes here, he found substantial variation in constituents seeking help with a problem by state size. Constituents from more populous states were much less likely to report seeking help with a problem or information from their Senators [@Oppenheimer1996].

How do we reconcile our intuition about greater population leading to greater constituent demand with the existing literature demonstrating constituents from less populous states receiving better representation? We think those studies are capturing representational outcomes, which are functions of the legislator's office capacity and member choices about what to prioritize. Thus we argue that representing more constituents will be associated with higher levels of interbranch representation. 

Before moving on to our next component of demand, we will note two complications that limit the conclusions we can draw about constituent population: 1) constituent population only meaningfully varies in the Senate, and 2) the amount of money senators receive to run their offices is a function of state population. Thus state population in the Senate is a somewhat bundled treatment that includes both increased population and an increased office budget.^[We do not know, and we make no claims about, whether the variation in funding senators receive is sufficient to compensate for the variation in constituent population.]

We turn next to our second form of constituent demand: **constituent need for government service.** To estimate district need, we use estimates of program utilization and employment from the U.S. Census. Constituents receiving public assistance may have a greater need for help from the federal government. To measure this form of constituent need, we use the estimated percent of people receiving public assistance or Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) from the U.S. Census. Similarly, we use the estimated percentage of employment in different sectors. <!--Greater employment in the private sector may generate more demand for constituency service on behalf of businesses. Employment in the nonprofit and government sectors may generate demand for constituency service on behalf of these employees. --> 

Constituent demand may vary for reasons other than population and underlying need for service. <!--As former Congressman and political scientist David E. Price noted when describing his experience representing North Carolina's fourth district, "...constituents vary considerably in their ability and inclination to use it" [@Price2022].--> 
A constituent encountering a problem with the federal bureaucracy needs to know that they can reach out to their congressional representatives for assistance with such problems, know how to do so, and then have the time and energy to follow through and reach out to them. None of the linkages in that chain should be taken for granted. A large body of work demonstrates that most Americans are ill-informed about how government works and that knowledge is unevenly distributed across the American public [@DelliCarpiniKeeter1996; @Lupia2016]. @Verba95's canonical Civic Voluntarism Model suggests that citizens need both the motivation and capacity to participate, with constituents with higher socio-economic status (particularly education) being most likely to speak up. Therefore, our last form of constituent demand is the **political savvy** of constituents in we which we focus on the constituents who might be most aware of the services that congressional offices offer and best able to advocate for themselves. Consistent with the Civic Volunteerism Model [@Verba95], we consider the percentage of highly educated constituents (bachelor's degree or higher). Similarly, because government employees are more likely to be aware of the services that congressional offices can provide, we also include the percentage of government employees in the district. 

Politically savvy constituents likely increase the demand for all types of work from a congressional office. However, high-capacity constituents may be higher policy demanders than constituency service demanders, leading to more policy-focused interbranch work in districts with more informed constituents. 


## Measuring Capacity


A number of different factors are likely to affect a legislator's capacity, or the ability of their office to produce work. These include factors that pertain to legislators themselves, such as their experience in office and their institutional positions, as well as factors related to the congressional office more broadly, like the number of staff and how staff are allocated across different tasks. We include all of these measures as different facets of capacity. 

### Legislator Experience 

Like anyone starting a new job, legislators face startup costs such as how to organize their office, develop efficient routines, and make connections. As @JudgeLordPowellGrimmer2026 documented, much of the startup costs (especially for constituency service) occur in the first two years of legislators' tenure. We thus model experience as having more than two years in office for purposes of testing the impact of experience against other causes of variation in interbranch representation. 
As a measure of relevant experience prior to taking office, we use an indicator of whether the legislator was a state legislator provided by @VoldenWiseman2014 and @VoldenWiseman2018. Almost half of members of Congress previously served as a state legislator.

### Committee Leadership Roles and Committee Oversight Relationships 

Committee chairs direct committee staff in addition to their own personal staff. Empirical research shows that this additional staff capacity increases both policy work [@Ritchie2018; @Ritchie2023; @JudgeLordPowellGrimmer2026] and constituency service [@JudgeLordPowellGrimmer2026]. 

All executive branch agencies "report" to one or more congressional committees charged with overseeing their work. Both chambers also have an "oversight" committee that focuses on a small number of investigations, usually of scandals or other alleged wrongdoing. Reporting committees are different. They may investigate perceived problems with the agencies they oversee. Indeed, oversight hearings --- the classic example of congressional oversight --- are often conducted by reporting committees. However, these committees also provide coverage over nearly the entire executive branch, dividing the work of monitoring and developing policy targeting particular agencies. Members of Congress have an especially close relationship with the agencies that report to their committees. 

Only a small proportion of Congress-agency interactions rise to the levels of hearings and investigations. Instead, as @Lowande2018APSR and @LowandePotter2021 demonstrate, most congressional interventions happen in direct communication between legislators and agencies. Legislators who sit on congressional committees overseeing an agency are likely to engage in higher levels of interbranch representation with that agency. We think this relationship is likely to exist for two reasons. First, legislators are likely to be substantively interested in that policy area to have received a seat on that committee. Second, their responsibility as committee members may also lead them to engage in higher interbranch representation with agencies under the committee's jurisdiction.  

To identify this link between agencies and legislators, we combine several sources of existing data and augment it with additional research into the committees members sit on. The result is a new dataset on committee assignments, including committee chair, ranking minority, subcommittee chair, and other leadership positions [updating @StewartWoon2017].^[Committee assignment and position data are available at <https://github.com/judgelord/committees>. We cross-checked and augmented these data with chair and subcommittee chair indicators compiled by @VoldenWiseman2014 and @VoldenWiseman2018 from the Almanac of American Politics.] <!--We adopt the definition of prestige committee assignments from @JudgeLordPowellGrimmer2026.--> 

Finally, we crosswalk reporting committee assignments with committee jurisdictions using the ACUS Sourcebook of United States Executive Agencies [@LewisSelin2012]. This gives us an indicator for each legislator-agency pair of whether the legislator sat on a reporting committee with oversight jurisdiction over that agency in each congress. We consider oversight relationships to be a measure of capacity (because legislators have special access to committee staff and information and may be more likely to get a response from the agencies that report to them) and strategic behavior (because legislators seek to join committees that oversee parts of the government they care about).

### Staff Volume and Allocation

While legislators may often sign letters to agencies, congressional staff do most of the work. Legislators who hire more staff may have more capacity to make more requests. And legislators who prioritize a certain type of activity may devote more staff resources to accomplish that objective [@Reynolds2020]. Thus, congressional offices that devote more resources to staff who do a certain type of work are likely to produce more of that type of work. 
We use staff budget data for members of the House from @CrossonFurnasLapiraBurgat2021, specifically Members' Representational Allowance (MRA) and the portion of MRA each member spent.^[Specifically, we use the @CrossonFurnasLapiraBurgat2021 data from the replication files for @CrossonKaslovsky2024.] These measures vary by Congress. 


## Measuring Incentives for Strategic Behavior

Legislators may strategically respond to their political environment in a number of ways, some of which may affect how they allocate their office capacity. As measurements of strategic behavior, we rely on legislators' staff allocation, ideological distance from federal agencies, electoral competitiveness, majority party status, and whether the legislator is a member of the president's party. The latter four factors are features of the political environment to which legislators are likely to respond strategically, while legislators' choices about staff allocation likely *reflect* strategic choices about the kind of work that they wish to prioritize. 

To assess the ideological similarity between members of Congress and each federal agency, we compare members' first dimension
DW-NOMINATE scores [@dwnominate2024] with survey-based measurements of federal
agencies' perceived ideological leanings [@RichardsonClintonLewis2018].
To measure the ideological **distance** between members of Congress and
federal agencies, we subtract each member’s first-dimension DW-NOMINATE
score from the ideology score of each agency.^[
Technically, 0 has no special meaning on these latent scales; therefore, for example, there is no reason that -1 and 1 are equally ideologically distant. However, the @RichardsonClintonLewis2018 scale is locally identified to have mean 0, so absolute value serves as a linear measure of distance from the mean. Moreover, agencies with ideological scores near zero include the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), and Veterans Benefits Administration (VBA), which are agencies that respondents presumably would perceive to be neither liberal nor conservative when responding to the survey question, suggesting 0 could be considered "moderate." @RichardsonClintonLewis2018 estimates subagency-specific perceived ideology scores for many sub-agencies in our data. For sub-agencies that do not have a specific score, we use their department's score. 
Six small, extremely low-salience independent agencies or commissions do not have a score. We assign them a score of 0. <!--This makes the measure of distance for these agencies the same as the absolute value of a member's first-dimension DW-NOMINATE score, which we control for in all models.-->  These six were 
the American Battle Monuments Commission (ABMC), 
the Court Services and Offender Supervision Agency (CSOSA),
National Capital Planning Commission (NCPA; despite making the news in 2026, it is reasonable to assume it did not have a strong partisan perception prior),
U.S. Nuclear Waste Technical Review Board, 
the Postal Regulatory Commission (PRC),
U.S. Railroad Retirement Board (RRB)
]
For example, Bernie Sanders, with a NOMINATE score of -0.545 (liberal), has a distance close to zero with the Department of Labor's Mine Health and Safety Administration with a score of -0.580 (liberal), but a distance close to 1 with the United States Trade Representative (USTR) with a score of 0.439 (conservative). 
The largest distance in our data is 2.66 between the Office of the Secretary of Defense and Joint Staff (1.91) and Carte Goodwin (-0.747).
To help guard against conclusions about distance being driven by distance from zero on the DW-NOMINATE scale, we control for the absolute value of the first dimension DW-NOMINATE. 
 We also use other legislator-level variables from @dwnominate2024, including party membership to derive majority status and whether a legislator is a member of the president's party. 

For data on electoral competitiveness, we use data from @Thomsen2023 on vote share in primary and general elections, adopting her definition of whether an election was competitive.

## Statistical Models {#sec-models}

<!--
[Are we planning to use different models to test demand, capacity, and strategy? If so, do we want to move the models to the results section for each type?]
Not yet in this version
--> 

Our analysis is generally at the legislator-agency-year level. <!--, with a few models at the district-agency-year level to examine changes in interbranch representation with electoral turnover. 
<!--Our hypotheses in @sec-theory set out expectations for differences across members and within-member variation.--> 
We estimate both cross-sectional and difference-in-differences regressions, similar to the specifications in @BerryFowler2016. 
Because our outcome is a count, we use negative binomial regression with agency-year fixed effects to estimate differences in interbranch representation across members of Congress (cross-sectional differences). To estimate within-legislator differences over time, we include legislator-agency fixed effects.^[We drop ten member-year level observations where members switched chambers mid-congress because the office resources of members of the House and Senate differ significantly and, thus, attributing their counts to either House or Senate in those years is not quite right.] 
Tests for differences within legislator-agency pairs take a form similar to @eq-full (with additional variables, such as those relating to primary elections, that decrease the number of observations included only in some specifications). 
However, to assess how much each factor contributes to the observed differences across members shown in @fig-percent-1, we must rely on cross-sectional estimates (@eq-full without $\gamma_{ij}$). 

We estimate all models separately for the House and the Senate, as well as pooled with an indicator to capture the capacity boost, including the staff allocation, that being a Senator provides. 

Most predictors are at the legislator-year level ($it$) while a few are at the legislator-agency-year level ($itj$). Predictors at the legislator level ($i$) like prior experience are not included in difference-in-differences models because there is no within-legislator variation.
When perceived ideological distance is included in models, we interact it with the indicator for whether the legislator has a co-partisan president ("president's party") because legislators may interact differently with aligned and unaligned agencies depending on their partisan alignment with the president. 


$$
\begin{aligned}
Y_{ijt}\mid X_{ijt},\gamma_{ij},\delta_{jt},m_{it},p_{it} &\sim \text{NegBin}(\mu_{ijt},\alpha),\\
\log(\mu_{ijt}) = \\
  & \underline{-Demand-}\\
  & \beta_1 \text{District Population}_{it}+\\
  & \beta_2 \text{Percent Goverment Workers}_{it}+\\
  & \beta_3 \text{Percent with College Degree}_{it}+\\
  & \beta_4 \text{Percent Receiving Public Assistance}_{it}+\\
  & \underline{-Capacity-}\\
  & \beta_5 \text{Experience in Congress}_{it}+\\
  & \beta_6 \text{Experience in State Legislator}_{it}+\\
  & \beta_7 \text{Staff Budget}_{it}+\\
  & \beta_8 \text{Committee Chair}_{it}+\\
  & \beta_{9}  \text{Subcommittee Chair}_{it}+\\
  & \beta_{10}  \text{Ranking Minority Committee Member}_{it}+\\
  & \beta_{11}  \text{Reporting Committee Member}_{itj}+\\
  & \underline{-Stratigic Environment-}\\
  & \beta_{12}  \text{Competitive Prior Election}_{it}+\\
  & \beta_{13}  \text{Republican}_{it}+\\
  & \beta_{14}  \text{President's Party}_{it}+\\
  & \beta_{15}  \text{Perceived Ideological Distance}_{itj}+\\
  & \beta_{16}  \text{President's Party} \times \text{Perceived Distance}_{it}+\\
  & \underline{-Other-}\\
  & \beta_{17}  \text{|DW-NOMINATE 1|}_{it}+\\
  &...\\
  & \gamma_{ij} + \delta_{jt} 
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-full}


$Y_{ijt}$ is the number of requests legislator $i$ makes to agency $j$ in year $t$. We estimate a negative binomial count model with conditional mean $\mu_{ijt}$ and overdispersion parameter $\alpha$. The conditional mean is linked to covariates via the log link, $\log(\mu_{ijt})$: a one-unit increase in a covariate multiplies the expected count by $\exp(\beta)$, holding other terms fixed.

$\gamma_{ij}$ denotes a *legislator--agency* fixed effect that is estimated using a true conditional fixed-effects approach (i.e., conditioned out rather than included as a full set of dummy variables). This fixed effect controls for time-invariant legislator characteristics and time-invariant legislator--agency-specific factors, including persistent constituent demand for assistance from a given agency and stable state or district attributes (population, demographics, local industries) that shape demand for particular agencies.

$\delta_{jt}$ is an agency-year fixed effect that accounts for agency-specific shocks over time that may affect the level of requests received from legislators in the periods for which data are available from each agency.


# Results {#sec-results}

This section presents results from the regression described in @eq-full. 
Because non-linear coefficients are difficult to interpret and because the total sample includes several additional agencies than the hand-coded samples, we present marginal effects in percentage terms.^[.Fixed effects regressions were estimated using the `fixest` R package [@fixest]. Average marginal effects are estimated using the delta method via the `avg_comparisons` from the `marginaleffects` R package [@marginaleffects].]
The full results are available in @tbl-models-full.^[We drop ten member-year level observations where members switched chambers mid-congress.] 

## Results: Demand

@fig-marginal-population shows the predicted marginal effects for a one standard deviation change in each of the demographic variables we use to measure constituent demand on each of our hand-coded types of interbranch representation provided by members of the House and Senate. Because we are interested in explaining variation across districts, and because these variables change little over time, we focus on cross-sectional models. However, models in the appendix, including  @tbl-models-demand_tot and @tbl-models-full-majority-tot, consistently show changes in district population causing changes in interbranch representation in the difference-in-differences specifications as well. 

Overall, more constituents, more needy constituents, and more demanding constituents are generally associated with more constituency service, but not more policy work (except for college graduates, which is associated more with policy work). Some of these relationships are very large.
The main takeaways from @fig-marginal-population are that (a) Legislators representing more constituents do more constituency service; (b) Senators with needier constituents do much more constituency service, especially for nonprofits (panel b, lower), but members of House with needier constituents only do slightly more for nonprofits (panel b, upper); (c) Members of the House representing more government workers do more constituency service, but Senators do not (d) Legislators representing more educated constituents do more policy work, but not necessarily more constituency service.
More specifically, Senators with more constituents do more interbranch work on behalf of all types of constituents, as well as more interbranch policy work (panel b, lower). The effects of state population on volume of constituency service are large (+35-40%). These effects can be partially explained by the capacity boost from the additional staff allocation that senators from larger states receive.  

By construction, House districts have nearly identical populations and office budget allocations.^[Representatives from more expensive districts receive budgets adjusted for renting more expensive office space, but not for paying higher district staff salaried.] Nevertheless, we see legislators from slightly larger House districts providing small but statistically significant additional volume of constituency service. This is solid support for @thm-hyp:demand with respect to demand coming from the number of constituents on represents.
As anticipated by @thm-hyp:demand, more needy constituents receive more constituency service, but only for the Senate. Members of the House from needier districts provide slightly more help to nonprofits, and senators provide a great deal more help to nonprofits. This mostly supports @thm-hyp:demand with respect to district need, with that relationship being much weaker for the House.

```{r}
#|   - "% Constituents Receiving Public Assistance or SNAP"
#|   - "% Constituents Employed by Government"
```

## Results: Capacity

The capacity gains that come with experience in Congress and committee positions have significant and often large effects on many forms of interbranch representation, especially policy work.
In addition to the effect of the number of constituents one represents, @fig-marginal-chamber shows large average differences between members of the House and Senate, with Senators doing more than twice the amount of all types of interbranch representation as Representatives, more than three times as much on behalf of nonprofits and local governments. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-marginal-chamber
#| fig-cap: "Differences by Chamber"
#| out-width: "50%"

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "marginal-chamber-1.png"))
```

Experience in Congress increases interbranch representation. Prior experience in state legislatures does not. 
@fig-marginal-experience (a) shows no evidence that prior experience in state legislatures is associated with more interbranch representation. Because prior legislative experience is a fixed attribute, we cannot estimate within-legislator variation, but we see no differences in the House or Senate. 
@fig-marginal-experience (b) shows strong effects of experience that are consistent in magnitude in within- and across-legislator comparisons. After their first two years in office Legislators do 15-20% more constituency service and 35-50% more policy work. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-marginal-experience
#| fig-cap: "Differences with Experience"
#| out-width: "100%"
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-subcap: 
#|   - "Experience in state legislature"
#|   - "Experience in the U.S. Congress"

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "marginal-state_leg-1.png"))
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "marginal-experience-1.png"))
```

Committee staff significantly boost non-legislative policy work.
@fig-marginal-committee shows that committee leadership positions increase interbranch policy work such as commenting on proposed agency rules and conducting oversight investigations. Subcommittee leadership positions do not, possibly because they cannot direct staff capacity as committee chairs and (often) ranking minority members can.
Serving on a committee to which an agency reports is associated with more constituency service and policy work, but this effect is only causal for policy work. The greater level of constituency service with agencies that legislators oversee (panel d, upper) likely reflects pre-existing interest in that agency that drove interest in joining that committee in the first place. 
Specifically, @fig-marginal-committee shows committee chairs doing more than twice the level of general interbranch policy work of non-chairs (panel 1, upper). Much of this cross-sectional difference is a causal effect, with legislators increasing the amount of policy work by over 75% when they gain a committee chair position (panel 1, lower). 
Differences in policy work on behalf of specific industries are much smaller (+25%) and not statistically significant in the within-legislator design. 
Gaining a committee chair position is associated with neither more nor less constituency service. 
Ranking Minority positions have similar effects at a slightly lesser scale for members of standing committees (panel b). Ranking members do 65% more policy work (panel b, upper), with most of that cross-sectional difference being a causal effect. When a legislator becomes a ranking member, they increase interbranch policy work by nearly 50% (panel b, lower). 
Again, differences in policy work on behalf of specific industries are much smaller (+25-30%) and not statistically significant in the within-legislator design. 
Subcommittee chair positions (panel c) are associated with much smaller and not statistically significant increases in interbranch representation. 
On top of chair effects, legislators who serve committees to which an agency reports (panel d, upper) do 
nearly double the amount of policy work with that agency and more constituency service with that agency (a small amount more individual constituency service to 35% more service on behalf of nonprofits and local governments). For general policy work, a good share of this effect is causal, with legislators who join a committee (panel d, lower) increasing policy work with that agency by 40%. Differences in constituency service and corporate policy work are not significant in the with-member design, suggesting that cross-sectional differences result from legislators who join the committees to which an agency reports are already doing constituency service and industry-specific policy work with that agency.

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Differences with Committee Positions"
#| out-width: "100%"
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-subcap: 
#|   - "Committee Chair"
#|   - "Ranking Minority Committee Member"
#|   - "Subcommittee Chair"
#|   - "Reporting Committee Position"

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "marginal-chair-1.png"))
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "marginal-ranking_minority-1.png"))
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "marginal-subchr-1.png"))
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "marginal-oversight-1.png"))
```

## Results: Strategic Behavior and the Political Environment

Electoral incentives do not appear to motivate interbranch work.
@fig-marginal-electoral shows little variation among legislators who face competitive general or primary elections. Members of the House who face competitive general elections do more interbranch constituency service on behalf of individuals and businesses (panel a, upper).
Senators whose prior general election was competitive do no more interbranch work and may even do less on behalf of nonprofits and local governments (panel a, lower).  
House districts with competitive primaries are not associated with more interbranch representation.^[In the difference in differences model (model 4 of @tbl-models-full-majority-ind), we do see members of the House doing more individual constituency service in years where their prior primary was competitive than when it was not. However, this effect is not constantly significant across specifications (e.g., @tbl-models-elect-ind).]

```{r}
#| label: fig-marginal-electoral
#| fig-cap: "Differences by Electoral Competitiveness"
#| out-width: "100%"
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-subcap: 
#|   - "Competitive General Election"
#|   - "Competitive Primary Election"

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "marginal-competitive-1.png"))
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "marginal-competitive_primary-1.png"))
```

Partisan and ideological incentives drive interbranch work in several ways that do not cleanly support either @thm-motivation. Instead, we find different parts of @thm-motivation supported for different kinds of interbranch work. 
The clearest takeaway is that legislators work with partisan/ideological allies in the executive branch when working on behalf of nonprofits and local governments. 
As expected, Republicans do significantly more corporate constituency service (@fig-marginal-partisan, panel a) --- nearly 40% more than Democrats on average. Interestingly, Republicans do not do significantly more policy work on behalf of businesses, but do significantly more constituency service (all else equal). This is likely due to the lower cost of living in districts represented by Republicans, allowing Republicans being able to hire more district staff despite allocating the same share of their budget, on average, to constituency service. 
Democrats do about 20% more interbranch work on behalf of nonprofits and local governments. Democrats also do about 20% more policy work on average. 
The story about partisan and ideological alignment or antagonism is more complicated. 
Supporting @thm-motivation 3a(+) @fig-marginal-partisan (b) shows legislators of the same party as the president doing more work on behalf of nonprofits and local governments, as well as more policy work on behalf of particular industries. Likewise, legislators do less work on behalf of nonprofits and local governments with agencies perceived as ideologically distant from them (panel c). However, in contrast to alignment with the president, alignment with the agency is associated with *less* corporate policy work (nearly 30% more policy work with one standard deviation greater perceived ideological distance) One possible explanation for this finding flowing from @thm-motivation 3a(+) is that legislative offices are doing policy work on behalf of certain industries by attacking regulators of those industries (e.g., conservatives spending time representing industry interests to the Environmental Protection Agency, which is perceived as ideologically distant). Thus, these results provide mixed support for both competing hypotheses about partisan/ideological effects under @thm-motivation, with nonprofit and local government service clearly driven by incentives to collaborate and some evidence for both collaborative- and oversight-rooted theories driving interbranch policy work.

# Discussion and Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

We find substantial variation across legislators in how much interbranch representation they provide to their constituents. A large share of this variation can be explained by legislator capacity, especially staff resources and experience in Congress. Committee staff capacity seems to be a major driver of variation in interbranch policy work. Legislators are also much more likely to do all types of interbranch representation with agencies in their committees' jurisdiction. We find mixed partisan and ideological effects, with strong evidence that legislators work with ideologically proximate agencies and co-partisan presidents on behalf of nonprofits and local governments. We find little evidence for theories that interbranch representation is reelection-motivated. Capacity-focused reforms --- larger staffs, stronger training, and better retention of experienced personnel --- may offer a promising lever for more equitable interbranch representation.

Examining interbranch representation reshapes our understanding of how Congress and the executive branch interact. Our models of interbranch relations (both in public discourse and formal theory) are largely based on a formal, constitutionally prescribed division of legislative and executive functions. Thus, political scientists have focused on legislative bargaining, delegation of policymaking authority, and oversight hearings. This focus neglects the primary way legislators interact with the executive branch. While certainly operating in the shadow of formal oversight, lawmaking, and budgeting powers, interbranch representation mostly relies on norms, relationships, and softer forms of legitimacy. From an interbranch representation perspective, "separation of powers" is a misleading moniker. The behavior we document involves formal and informal mechanisms by which legislators influence how the executive branch makes and implements policy on a daily basis. There are a few executive branch activities that Members of Congress do not involve themselves in, and any lack of involvement is likely due to a lack of capacity rather than any formal separation of powers on paper. 

Future research could examine other forms of interbranch representation, such as members of Congress submitting amicus briefs for court cases. Future work could also build on existing work on oversight hearings as a form of representation [@Minta2011] and other ways that members of Congress engage in bureaucratic decision-making, such as participating in advisory committees. 
One form of interbranch representation present in our data but excluded from our analysis is correspondence with White House officials, as well as lobbyists, suggesting that agencies' congressional offices are situated in a constellation of external political relationships that agencies need to manage. Notably, White House officials sometimes played a similar ombudsman role as congressional offices. 

As a practical matter, the institutions of our vast federal government cannot magically coordinate and work together to solve problems. Interbranch correspondence is work that stitches the government together. The "three branches" of government metaphor may do harm to our understanding of a complex federal system [@Bednar2009] with stylized job descriptions. The threads of scholarship we tried to unite in this book paint a richer picture of what representation is in practice with our institutions as they are. A bureaucracy of millions serving a population of hundreds of millions will always do so imperfectly, with opportunities for improvement inspired by people's problems, and inevitable fights over policy continuing long after the ink is dry on most pieces of legislation. Businesses, universities, and local governments will always be searching for someone with clout to get their bid or application a second look. 

Our findings emphasizing the importance of experience and the number of office and committee staff suggest that researchers should ask questions typically asked of bureaucracies, such as how staff is selected and deployed and the consequences of these decisions [@Brierley2023]. For example, journalists have suggested that a member replacing their office staff with former White House officials gives it stronger ties to the president [@Weiner2023]. If institutional structure and access to staff drive differences in representation,  scholarship on bureaucratic organization of Congress, allocation of resources to different tasks [@Ommundsen2025], and capacity [@CrossonFurnasLapiraBurgat2021] takes on new importance.
